title: Listening in Kalyan
hookLine: a bee that keeps coming back, a bird that waits for one drop: reading along with a short hymn of Guru Arjan in Kalyan

lines: A BEE THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.
A HYMN SHORT ENOUGH TO READ ALONG.
cards: A bumblebee on a lavender bush doesn't land once and leave. It circles, and comes back to the same flower, again and again. Nobody has to persuade it; something there is sweet enough.

Kalyan, the evening raga, holds hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and one of Guru Arjan's is built around that bee. It's short enough to read from start to finish, so today it gets read slowly, line by line.

teach.b: The hymn opens with its center line, the one marked Rahao, pause. In paraphrase: grant me this grace, that like the bee drawn to the nectar of the lotus, my mind is drawn to your lotus feet, again and again.
In Gurmukhi, again and again is fer fer, and you can hear it turning back on itself. That's the whole prayer of the hymn: not one visit, but a mind that keeps returning.
The first verse brings in a bird, the chatrik, the rainbird from Malar's rain pictures, which tradition says drinks only drops of rain.
In paraphrase: I have no business with any other water; give this rainbird the drop of the Lord.
The second verse closes it: without meeting, there is no contentment; seeing the vision, Nanak lives. Guru Arjan signs the hymn with the name Nanak. Now hear it with Kalyan's evening around it.
The bee isn't calm because it stopped moving. It's calm because it knows where it's going back to. The rainbird isn't calm because it's full; it knows which drop it's waiting for.
Contentment here, santokh, isn't having everything.

teach.h: PEACE IS BEING TURNED TOWARD ONE THING.
teach.b: It's being turned toward one thing.
That's a peace an evening can hold: not an empty room, but a mind that has found its flower and keeps landing there. Read it once, and when you hear Kalyan sung, you'll know where the bee is.

how: Sikhs often read a shabad with a translation open while it is sung in kirtan; some gurdwaras project the Gurmukhi and an English rendering on a screen so the congregation can follow line by line.

o: reading along with Guru Arjan's short hymn of the returning bee
listening for the drum pattern that marks a raga's evening hour
learning to sing every Kalyan hymn from memory in one evening

games.q: who's in Guru Arjan's Kalyan hymn — tap the pairs.
p: drawn to the lotus again and again
wants only the drop of the Lord

s: the rainbird in the hymn will take any water it can find
it has no business with any other water; it asks only for the drop of the Lord.
the bee hymn asks for a mind that keeps returning
drawn to the lotus feet again and again: fer fer.

games.q: you're the rainbird in Guru Arjan's hymn. a river runs nearby, full of water. what do you ask for?
o: only the drop of the Lord.
nothing at all: you'd rather stay thirsty.
games.why: the hymn says: I have no business with any other water; give this rainbird the drop of the Lord.

practice: If you can, find this hymn of Guru Arjan in Kalyan with a translation beside it, and read it once, slowly, while it's sung or in silence.
Then sit and choose one thing to return to: the breath at the nostrils or, if you pray, the word Waheguru.
The mind will wander, and the bee wanders too; each time you notice, come back to the same place, gently, without counting and without scolding.

wordCard.voice: Listening in Kalyan. Reading along with Guru Arjan's short hymn: the bee drawn to the lotus again and again, and the rainbird asking for one drop. Today's word.

orig.note: again and again: the bee's return to the lotus in Guru Arjan's Kalyan hymn.

carryVoice: Your line: evening peace. It isn't having everything; it's being turned toward one thing. See you tomorrow.
